title: A business without published numbers
lede: FilmStruck was a small line inside Turner, which was a division of Time Warner and then of AT&T. None of them reported its subscribers, revenue or costs. What follows is what can be counted: films, prices, signatures, and the size of the company that closed it.

blocks.subtitle: Films available on the U.S. service, as the press reported them. The counts come from different outlets and are not measured the same way.

blocks.title: What it cost, beside what came before and after
blocks.subtitle: U.S. monthly prices in dollars, as reported at each service’s launch or closure.
blocks.source: MUBI, as The Verge described it in November 2016.[^7] FilmStruck tiers.[^4] The annual plan was $99; $8.25 a month is derived ($99 ÷ 12).[^4] Warner Archive’s price when it closed in February 2018.[^12] Criterion Channel prices.[^35] HBO Max at launch.[^37] The British FilmStruck Curzon cost £5.99 a month and is left off because it was priced in pounds.[^11]

blocks.title: A year for the price of nine months

left.label: a year of FilmStruck with the Criterion Channel[^4]

unit.label: one month on the monthly plan

blocks.equation: $99 ÷ $10.99 ≈ 9.0. Paying monthly for a year would have cost $131.88, so the annual plan saved $32.88. Both prices are from Variety.[^4]

items.label: Everything else
items.note: about 1,200: Criterion, Janus and other licensed libraries

blocks.source: Variety, February 26, 2018: “more than 600 classic Hollywood films each month” and a lineup of “more than 1,800 movies per month, up from around 1,200.”[^12] The shares are derived, 600 ÷ 1,800 and 1,200 ÷ 1,800, and are approximate because both figures are lower bounds.

blocks.title: How small was niche?
blocks.subtitle: People, on four different measures. FilmStruck’s bar is an outside estimate; the owners never published a figure.

items.label: Netflix subscribers, late 2018
items.note: As The Ringer put it: “in the neighborhood of 137 million”[^31]

items.label: Americans aged 18–49 Turner thought would be interested
items.note: Turner’s own estimate from a 2016 survey of 2,000 film fans[^4]

blocks.source: The Ringer[^31], Variety[^4], Change.org[^25] and the Los Angeles Times.[^23] On these figures the estimated subscriber base was under 1% of the audience Turner had projected (derived: 100,000 ÷ 15,000,000 ≈ 0.7%), and Netflix was about 1,370 times larger (derived).

blocks.title: The petition, signature by signature
blocks.subtitle: “Keep FilmStruck Alive” on Change.org, at the counts the press reported and the count on the page today.
blocks.source: 5,000 “two days ago” and “over 11,000”: Paste, November 1.[^21] “Over 40,000”: Variety, November 9.[^24] “Over 50,000”: /Film, November 15.[^27] “More than 55,000”: The Hollywood Reporter, November 16.[^30] 106,696: the petition page as we read it on October 8, 2026.[^25] The first five are lower bounds as reported, not exact counts. The petition was created on October 26, 2018, according to the date in the page’s data.[^25]

blocks.title: What AT&T paid Time Warner’s shareholders
blocks.subtitle: Implied value of the consideration at the closing price on June 14, 2018, $ billions.
blocks.source: AT&T Inc., Form 8-K filed June 15, 2018.[^15] This is the consideration paid to shareholders only. The Los Angeles Times described the deal as an “$85.4-billion merger”; the two figures measure different things and we have not reconciled them.[^22]

blocks.title: The company FilmStruck ended up inside

items.text: and more in 2017 revenue for HBO, Turner and Warner Bros. together, by AT&T’s account[^16]
and more direct-to-consumer relationships AT&T claimed on the day the deal closed[^16]
a year at most from 100,000 subscribers at $10.99 a month: an illustration built on an estimate, not a reported figure (derived)[^4][^23]
what that would be of the media business’s 2017 revenue (derived)[^16]

blocks.source: AT&T press release on the completion of the merger.[^16] The last two counters are derived: 100,000 × $10.99 × 12 = $13.19M, and $13.19M ÷ $31,000M ≈ 0.04%. They assume the Los Angeles Times estimate was right[^23] and that every subscriber paid the top monthly price[^4], so they are a ceiling on U.S. subscription revenue under that estimate, not a measurement.
